answer_text: Mr. Johnson chose the surname "Douglass," suggested by the "Lady of the Lake," which he had just been reading.

Order was the hardest virtue for Franklin to acquire.

- It is number 3 in his list, with the precept: "Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time" (evidence [3]).
- Franklin says "My scheme of Order gave me the most trouble" (evidence [17]).
- He had not been early accustomed to it, and having an exceedingly good memory, he was not so sensible of the inconvenience of want of method (evidence [8]).
- It cost him much painful attention, his faults vexed him, he made little progress and had frequent relapses, so he was almost ready to give up the attempt (evidence [8]).
- In truth, he found himself incorrigible with respect to Order, and even in old age, with bad memory, he feels the want of it (evidence [12]).

Faraday makes the water visible by placing a chimney over the candle: the moisture appears on it, which he identifies as water produced by the action of the air on the candle's hydrogen (evidence [6], Lecture V). To show carbonic acid, he points out that something non-condensable goes out at the top of the chimney, and that this air is nearly strong enough to blow out a light held to it, and will blow it quite out if opposed to the current (evidence [6], Lecture V). He also collects the products in a bucket and tests it with a taper, showing it is full of carbonic acid, which extinguishes the flame (evidence [10], Lecture V). Finally, he shows that water in which the gas is dissolved tastes slightly acid and turns lime-water turbid and white, proving the presence of carbonic acid (evidence [12], Lecture V).

Frederick Douglass - model: the ship carpenters' letters marked on timber at Durgin and Bailey's ship-yard, and the Italics in Webster's Spelling Book; practise: writing with a lump of chalk on the board fence, brick wall, and pavement, getting lessons from boys by challenging them, and copying Master Thomas's writing in the spaces left in his copy-book until he could write a hand very similar to Master Thomas's.

Benjamin Franklin - model: NOT_FOUND (evidence says he improved the method of the language and acquired ability in writing, but no specific model is named); practise: exercises and reading at night after work or before it began in the morning, or on Sundays when he contrived to be in the printing-house alone.

Both were self-taught: Douglass practised secretly with chalk on fences, walls, and pavement and by copying his master's copy-book, while Franklin practised writing exercises in his spare time at the printing-house, and writing was "of great use" to Franklin and "a principal means of my advancement."

Benjamin Franklin - signing indentures: twelve years old
Frederick Douglass - leaving Colonel Lloyd's plantation for Baltimore: probably between seven and eight years old

Frederick Douglass was younger, at between seven and eight years old, compared with Franklin's twelve years old.
